seriesTitle: The Reckoner of the Thirteenth Hour
title: Chapter 10: Figures at the Guild Door
blurb: Petra wins the Daylight Playoff on the Ninth Stair, opens the clock that cost her a post, and at dawn is asked to audit the Reserve.

blocks.text: Drewe's hands stayed flat on my blotter. I watched them because I could not yet trust my voice, and because they were the steadiest thing in front of me. The left thumb had clock oil on it. The right forefinger had an old cut across the pad, healed white.
'He won't be watching the box,' she said. 'He can't see in my pocket. Mr Wardle will be watching my collar. He'll wait for my hand to come up.'
'And if it doesn't come up?'
'Then he waits.' She looked at me for the first time since she had put the box down. 'He won't call an Audit on a guess. Not with two points on it.'

She was right about the price, and I knew it from the printed page. An Audit weighs both jars against the Tally, and if both are clean, the side that called it gives away two points. Wardle would not spend two points on a guess any more than I would.
'So you carry it on to the landing,' I said, 'and you don't wind it, and you don't touch your collar.'
'All match.' She took her hands off the desk at last and put them in her lap. 'I'll be wound tighter than a carriage clock. You'll have to forgive me if I tick.'
'And afterwards. Mabry.'
'Afterwards is afterwards.' She picked up the box and put it back in her coat. 'He'll know by the Close. That's mine to carry too.'

I wanted to tell her what to do about Mabry. I wanted to write it down for her, the way I had written Marguerite's three o'clocks and her own half-past-ones, so that it was in my hand and not hers. I did not. It was her coat the box was in.
'I have an Audit too,' I said. 'You told me he has couriers. More than one.'
'He's got more of us than me. We don't meet. That's the point of us.'
'Then I'll watch their Winder. The way you showed me.'
She nodded and went down the stair. My verdict, which I kept to myself, was the one I had come to on the landing that evening: Mabry did not pay for a side he was not also filling.

The playoff was the next midnight. I came off the night desk at six in the morning and walked to the east gate, where the Rate Board for the Ninth Stair landing had gone up at midnight, twenty-four hours ahead, as the printed Laws require. Plate XII, our Hour plate, was posted at one and a half, which suited Bao. Plate VI, theirs, was posted at three-quarters, which suited nobody.

Bao slept on the landing bench from noon until half past ten that night. At the pre-match check he wrote twenty-one and a half on the Arbiter's sleep ledger, and it was true, and the Arbiter wrote 'At or below' beside it.
Marguerite came up the stair at half past eleven with her hands in her pockets.
'Two coppers says Wardle's hand goes up before round six,' she said. 'Not for the Audit. To his hair. He does it when he's losing.'
'Nobody's taking that,' said Drewe.
'Nobody ever takes my good ones.'
The stroke came at midnight, and we were inside it.

The Sleepless Hands stood on the far side of the Arbor, five of them, in grey jerseys with nothing on the chest. Felix Wardle stood at their rail with their jar in both hands. He was younger than I had pictured him, with a neat beard and a pencil behind his ear. He did not look at me. He looked at Drewe.
Drewe walked on to the landing with Mabry's box in her coat and a Winder's place on the team sheet, and kept her hands at her sides.

I did not watch Wardle. I watched their Winder. Marguerite had named him on the stair: Danby, who had wound for the Copper Stair in her second season and had never once, she said, bought a round. He was a big man with soft hands, and he stood behind their Keep's plate with both of them in his coat pockets.
I had one Audit. If I called it on a jar that weighed clean, the Sleepless Hands had two points from me, and in a match we had to win to keep a League place, two points was the match.
The Token started round one on plate I, one stride from Bao.
'Marguerite, ten,' I said.
'Held.'

Ten was for the look of it. Wardle called Pell, their quicker Sprinter, for thirty. Pell said 'Spend', and I was frozen, as I am in every Lull. When it ended the Token lay on plate XII beside Bao's boot and Pell was on his knees on dead floor between XII and XI, breathing hard. The Tally had moved twenty-seven.
'Came round my back,' Bao said, while the Arbiter checked the Token. 'I turned. Touched his shoulder. Down it went, dead. Mm.'
A Spilled Token never scores on the plate where it was Spilled. Pell had nothing left to carry it off and back on. No score.

In the first Bank minute I wrote six on my slate. Wardle wrote four. The Arbiter turned them together, and the bank point was ours. Wardle took the pencil from behind his ear and made a mark on the edge of his slate, which was what Marguerite had said he did on the Copper Stair roofs.
In the second Bank minute he wrote seventeen. I wrote nought. Her slates said that after a lost point he went ten or more over his last bid, and he went thirteen over.

It went like that. Before every Bank minute I looked at what he had written last and what he had lost last, and whenever his slate was going to be a low one I beat it by a few seconds, and whenever he was chasing I let him have it for nothing. Every Bank minute, before he wrote, Wardle looked at Drewe's collar. Drewe stood at our rail with her hands flat on it. Once, in round six, she lifted her right hand to push her hair back, and Wardle's pencil stopped on the slate. She put the hand back on the rail. He started writing again. Marguerite said nothing, but I saw her mouth go tight.

The Sleepless Hands ran in rounds two and three, near starts both, and scored both times. I learned how from Bao afterwards, because his Set Still sprang each time and he saw what happened on his plate. 'Two of them both times,' he said. 'Screen on my left. I turned the wrong way once.' He thought about it. 'Twice.'

Marguerite ran in rounds seven and eight, both near starts, and scored both times. The far starts she was keeping for the end, where Wardle would have nothing left to meet them with. She came back to our rail the second time and said, 'Two coppers says that one hurt him,' and nobody took that either.
After eight rounds the board read Sleepless Hands nine, Ninth Stair seven. They had two runs and five bank points. We had two runs and three bank points.

And the Tally read like this. The Sleepless Hands had spent a hundred and thirty-one seconds and banked a hundred and forty-one. Their Issue was three hundred. Banked seconds sit in the jar's locked chamber until the Close and cannot be issued again. That left Wardle twenty-eight seconds to spend in four rounds. We had spent a hundred and twenty-four and banked thirty-eight. We had a hundred and thirty-eight.
That was the plan Marguerite's slates had given us, and it had worked. Four rounds were left, three of them far starts for her, and Wardle had almost nothing to run with.
Danby had kept his hands in his pockets for eight rounds. My verdict, by then, was that I had been wrong about him, and Mabry had only one box on that landing, and it was in Drewe's coat.
Round nine started on plate IX.
'Pell, twenty,' Wardle called.
'Held.'

It was most of what he had. In live play, before anyone spent, Danby walked across to plate X, where Pell stood, took one hand out of his pocket and laid it on Pell's wrist. The other hand stayed in his coat.
'Steady,' he said. 'You're all right.'
Pell had not stumbled. Danby let go, walked to Strake on plate IX, and did the same: one hand in the coat, the other on the wrist. 'Steady.'
It was what Drewe had shown me at my desk, with her own hand on my wrist.
I looked at Drewe. She was looking at Danby's coat. Her hands were flat on the rail and her face had gone the colour of the wall.
Wardle had called no seconds for Strake.

Strake said 'Spend'. I was frozen. When I could see again, the Token lay dead on plate XII, Pell was standing next to Bao on XII with his hands empty, and Strake was on XI with his hands on his thighs. The Tally had moved thirty-seven.
Bao told it plainly. 'Strake came on first, with it. I touched him. Dead. Then Pell, still going. Picked it up, stepped off on to eleven, came back on. I touched him too. Then he'd nothing left.'
'Strake ran,' I said. 'All the way from IX.'
'Mm. From nine.'

I wrote it down. Wardle had called twenty, all of it to Pell. Danby had never touched Pell and Strake at the same time. No called second had been wound from one man to the other. Thirty-seven had gone up on the Tally. Seventeen seconds had been spent, or burnt as friction, that nobody issued. The board now read a hundred and sixty-eight spent and a hundred and forty-one banked: three hundred and nine, against an Issue of three hundred.
No clean jar can spend and bank more than it was given.
The Bank minute began. Wardle looked at the board. Then he looked at Danby. Then he looked at Drewe's collar, and Drewe's hands did not move.
I was afraid. I watched Wardle's hands, because they were nearest. They were flat on the lid of his jar, the thumbs pressed white against the catch-brass seal.
I put my hand up.
'Audit,' I said.

The Arbiter came to the Arbor scale. She took our jar first, because I had called it, and read from her sheet in a flat voice. 'Ninth Stair. Issue three hundred. Spent one hundred and twenty-four. The jar should hold one hundred and seventy-six.' She set it on the scale. 'One hundred and seventy-six.' She put her bare palm on the glass. 'Cold.'
I looked at our rail. Drewe's hands were still flat on it, with the oil on the left thumb.
'Tamsin,' I said.
It was the first time I had used it. She heard it. She nodded once and did not move her hands.
The Arbiter took Wardle's jar from him. He held on to it a moment longer than he needed to, and then let go.

'Sleepless Hands. Issue three hundred. Spent one hundred and sixty-eight. The jar should hold one hundred and thirty-two.' She set it on the scale. 'One hundred and fifty-four.' She put her palm on the glass and kept it there. 'Warm. Twenty-two over. Pool Fraud. The match is forfeited to the Ninth Stair.'
Wardle took the pencil from behind his ear and put it in his pocket. Then his hand went up to his hair and stayed there. Marguerite saw it. She did not claim her two coppers.

The Arbiter asked Danby to empty his coat on to the Arbor rail. He did it slowly. A handkerchief, a tram ticket, three new coins, and a brass snuffbox. She opened the lid. There was a card inside, in round copybook letters: wind times, and against round nine, 'ten and ten'.
That gave me the split, and I wrote it under my figures while she read.
Two transfers of ten, friction one each: two seconds the Tally counted that never came out of their jar. Twenty seconds wound in.

Twenty-two over on the scale, against seventeen of unissued Tally on the board, meant five of those twenty were in a Sprinter's hand unspent when the round ended, and went back into the jar still warm. The other fifteen were spent, showed on the Tally, and never left the jar either. Two and fifteen and five. Twenty-two.

She put the card in an envelope and wrote on the envelope. Then she looked along our rail. Tamsin's hands were flat on it. The Arbiter looked at our jar, which had weighed to the second, and turned back to Danby.

Marguerite had not said a word since round nine. She was looking at Wardle, and Wardle was looking at the floor, and she went on looking at him the whole time the Arbiter wrote. That was how I knew she was frightened, even then.
The Ninth Stair kept its place in the Stairwell League.

At the Close in the porter's lodge the spot-check clerk weighed our jar on the Bank's scale, zero checked. One hundred and seventy-six, cold. I wrote Marguerite's hundred and twenty-four minutes into her three o'clocks, and she said yes to every line. There was nothing to book for Tamsin. She had wound nothing all night.
The next afternoon Tamsin came up the stair with her coat over her arm and turned the pockets out on the bench without being asked. They were empty except for the screwdriver.
'Gone,' she said.
Marguerite looked at the empty pockets and then at her. 'Two coppers says you threw it in the millrace.'
'Two coppers says you'll never know,' said Tamsin, and Marguerite laughed for the first time since the Close.
I did not ask where. When I first came to that landing I would have asked, and written the answer down, and then it would have been mine. It was hers.
'Good,' I said, and she put her coat back on.

Mabry's hearing sat three days later. The notice on the door said the Board chamber had been lent to the Bank of Hours for the day. It was a long cold room beneath the Bank, with a round table and thirteen chairs. Twelve had names carved into their backs. The thirteenth was plain wood. I looked at it for some time. Nobody else in the room looked at it at all.

A Bank officer read the finding. Danby's box was catch-brass. The card in its lid was in Dunstan Mabry's hand, which three witnesses swore to. Danby would go before the Arbiters' Court on the catch-brass charge. Mabry's licence as a sponsor was withdrawn from that day.
Mabry thanked the officer. He asked after her daughter's examinations, by name. He said it had all been a little arrangement, and he was sorry it had come to paper.
In the corridor afterwards he stopped beside me with his hat in his hands.
'No hard feelings, Miss Sandor,' he said. 'And that card in your drawer. Nothing personal in it, my dear. Nothing about you at all, really.'
He went down the corridor turning the hat round by its brim.

My verdict was that a man who had written one sentence to me in his life was now telling me what it did not mean, and that meant it did. I believed the post had gone to Orme because of my father, and that Mabry knew it.

That night I logged the Guild Hall tram-stop clock as a fault, two minutes slow against my watch, which the night desk may do for any public clock, and went down to it with a lamp and the case key. The stop was empty. It was a quarter past two.

The escapement should have been steel. The Guild's register says steel for every clock of that pattern. It was brass, pale and finely cut, and when I put my bare finger to the rim of the scape wheel, between beats, it was warm, the way Tamsin's box had been warm.

Every Guild public clock carries a brass plate inside its case door, stamped at each order. The last line on this one was order nine of my forty: the number, 'Escapement renewed', a date two years back, and the initials C.O.

Works on a public clock come before the Night Audit two years after they are done. It is the first rule of the desk I had been promised. I knew the date of the committee's letter that took the post from me, because I had read it standing up and not sat down again for an hour. Order nine fell due for the Night Audit one week before that letter.

I had one plate. I had forty order numbers, all signed C. Orme, all sealed, all sent to the desk that should have been mine. The Senior Night Auditor opens those orders. Orme could not have me opening them. That was why the post went to him.
It was not my father. Mabry had said it was nothing about me, and it was the one true thing he had told me. I had been wrong about the reason, and I said so, out loud, to an empty tram stop.

I went back to the Guild and took the forty sealed orders out of the closed cabinet. I am allowed to file them. I am not allowed to open them, and I did not need to. Catch-brass in any hands but the Bank's is a crime under the printed Laws. The Arbiters' Court must hear a charge in open hearing within fourteen days. I could have had Orme in front of three Arbiters before the month was out.
I stood at the night desk with the orders in my hands and did not move.

I asked myself who else a report would sink. Tamsin, who had carried a box for months and whose name was on no card yet. The two rulings I had signed under, with forty-seven and thirty-five in my own hand. The draw and the win those rulings let stand. Whoever I had not thought of yet, which is always the one that matters.
I know what a report does to the people standing next to the name on it. I stood there until the windows went grey, and then I put the orders back in the cabinet and locked it.
Severine Holt was waiting at the Guild door at dawn. She was alone. She did not come in.
'Good morning, Miss Sandor,' she said. 'I haven't come about your playoff.'
I watched her hands. They were in her coat pockets, where I could not see them.

'The Reserve stands thirty-six thousand seconds above the Floor,' she said. 'Without the irregular inflows the Bank can no longer count on, it loses forty thousand a year. That is eleven months. On the first midnight it stands below the Floor, the Hour does not open. Thirteen such nights, and it never opens again.'
'And the Ninth Stair with it.'
'And every stair with it.' She said it the way she would have read me a rate. 'I have the Bank's figures, and I do not trust the people who gave them to me.'
She took her hands out of her pockets then. They were empty, and perfectly still.
'I would like you to audit the Reserve for me, Miss Sandor,' she said.
